/content/a76721db-36e1-4198-aad8-8c90137.title: Chevron pledges $7bn to double its Venezuela oil production
articleContent: Chevron plans to invest $7bn to more than double its oil production in Venezuela over the next five years, in the first big commitment from a US major in the Latin American country since the Trump administration toppled former leader Nicolás Maduro.

The White House has been pushing international companies to invest in Venezuela as it attempts to increase the supply of US-controlled oil from the country. Energy secretary Chris Wright is visiting Caracas this week to announce commitments by US groups and drum up further investment.

Chevron said on Wednesday that it had agreed new terms for its operations with state oil company PDVSA and that investment plans through its various joint ventures in the country would boost output to 600,000 barrels a day. The Houston-based group added it had secured the rights to develop two new oilfields in the Carabobo region within the oil-rich Orinoco belt.

Mike Wirth, Chevron’s chief executive, said the decision to expand its business in Venezuela “reflects our confidence in the country’s deep resource potential” and said the country would be a competitive part of its portfolio “for decades”.

Chevron said Venezuelan crude, which can often be heavy and difficult to extract and transport, would incur total costs of less than $20 a barrel. Its new acreage sits adjacent to existing joint venture holdings.
The company was among those to maintain its operations in Venezuela despite US sanctions and was seen by Washington as a block against Russia and China’s growing control in the country’s oil sector.
Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.
US majors ExxonMobil and ConocoPhillips have thus far been reluctant to make a move into Venezuela after losing billions of dollars’ worth of assets in state expropriations.

Italy’s Eni and Spain’s Repsol also kept operating in the country under US sanctions. Eni has said it could raise oil output from 12,000 b/d to 200,000 b/d or more but has not confirmed an investment plan.

The Trump administration this week defended its separate venture to boost Venezuela’s oil sector. Alejandro Betancourt, who owns the second-largest private oil company in Venezuela and is a polarising figure in the country, is the US’s partner in a group that will control about one-fifth of the Latin American nation’s oil reserves.

Betancourt’s company has begun looking for potential investors in the 17 oilfields it has access to with the goal of attracting $100bn in investment to the country. The Chevron deal is not linked to those efforts.

Chevron’s current production in the country is 280,000 barrels a day, up from 50,000 barrels a few years ago, analysts at RBC Capital said in a note this week after a meeting with the company’s chief financial officer Eimear Bonner.
Bonner said that “fiscal protections” like international arbitration rights would be needed for Chevron to invest more in Venezuela, the analysts added.
BP and Shell have both announced new projects in Venezuela this year, with most of their new investments focused on offshore gasfields.

macro_summary.paragraph_summary: Chevron has committed $7bn to more than double its oil production in Venezuela to 600,000 barrels a day within five years, marking the first major US energy investment in the country since the Trump administration began pushing for increased US-controlled oil output. The move, backed by US government pressure and aimed at countering Russian and Chinese influence, includes new rights to develop two oilfields in the Orinoco belt and relies on fiscal protections like international arbitration. The investment signals a shift in US energy strategy in Latin America, though other US majors remain cautious due to past losses from expropriations.
bullet_summary: Chevron plans $7bn in investment to more than double its Venezuelan oil output to 600,000 barrels a day within five years.
The move follows US government pressure to boost US-controlled oil production in Venezuela and counter Russian and Chinese influence.
Chevron secured rights to develop two new oilfields in the Orinoco belt and already produces 280,000 b/d, up from 50,000 b/d.
The company cited low production costs (under $20/bbl) and long-term confidence in Venezuela’s resource potential.
Other US majors like ExxonMobil and ConocoPhillips remain hesitant due to past asset seizures, while Eni, Repsol, BP, and Shell have maintained or expanded operations under sanctions.

/content/c74c483e-82ff-4b53-b59b-2404e65.title: Pentagon chaos deepens after Driscoll quits in clash with Hegseth
articleContent: US Army secretary Dan Driscoll handed his resignation to Donald Trump on Monday with a blunt message about Pete Hegseth’s interference with the largest branch of America’s military.

The departure of the army’s top civilian official was the culmination of months of tension with the defence secretary about the force’s technological transformation and senior military appointments, as well as intractable personal tensions between the two men.
Driscoll, a close friend of vice-president JD Vance, believed Hegseth was causing “generational damage” to the largest branch of the US military, according to a person familiar with his thinking.

He “had tried so many different ways and so many different times, but it was just clear that . . . Hegseth wasn’t willing to listen to the facts or the truth, or the reason, or any of that, because of his personal animosity”, the person said.

Driscoll’s exit brings another bout of turmoil to a Pentagon that has been rocked by infighting and Hegseth’s purge of top brass as the US struggles to end an extended conflict with Iran that is straining resources and depleting munitions.
“It’s a revelatory moment, and I think it illustrates that the Pentagon is in disarray,” said Tom Wright, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution.

Hegseth has purged two dozen generals and admirals since the start of Trump’s second term through firings or forced removals. In April, he sacked army chief of staff General Randy George, which became one of the biggest flashpoints between Driscoll and Hegseth.

Driscoll’s exit leaves the army, which is playing a crucial missile-defence role with its Patriot and Thaad batteries, with a leadership vacuum amid the Iran war, which has involved lengthy deployments to the Middle East for thousands of troops.
His decision to quit had been expected for weeks but was nonetheless seen by critics as a symbol of the chaos and drift at the defence department during Trump’s second term.

“Driscoll seemed to be one of the few senior civilian political leaders who was relatively level-headed and had the trust and confidence of the troops, and actually did a competent job,” said Christopher Meagher, a senior Pentagon official in the Biden administration.
He added that the lack of a permanent army secretary or chief of staff — posts that both require Senate confirmation — was “a serious leadership gap, especially in a time of war”.
A spokesperson for Hegseth referred a request for comment to the army. In a statement, Driscoll said he would step down on Wednesday.

“I had the privilege of working . . . to modernise and accelerate how the Army mans, trains, and equips the most lethal fighting force on the face of the earth,” he wrote on X. “We could not have made the progress we did without the support of Secretary Hegseth.”
Driscoll’s exit has even unnerved some Republicans. Mike Rounds, a senator from South Dakota, told reporters on Tuesday that he was “disappointed” by the departure.
“Where is the leadership at?” Rounds said. “We’ve had some very good generals that are no longer there that we respected.”

Hegseth has installed vice-chief of staff General Christopher LaNeve to serve as the army’s top commander on a temporary basis. But he wants LaNeve, a close ally, to have the job permanently. The appointment became another point of friction with Driscoll.

Some Senate Republicans, unhappy with how George was fired, have signalled LaNeve is unlikely to be confirmed. Driscoll’s departure after 18 months at the Pentagon is expected to add to their concerns.

“The opposition . . . is not about LaNeve himself. It’s about Hegseth, and the anger that is very much still alive on Capitol Hill over General George’s exit and Hegseth running roughshod over the army,” said a congressional aide.

Driscoll leaving would “create problems” for the Pentagon as it tries to sell a $1.5tn budget and tens of billions in supplemental funding for the war in Iran, the aide added. “Congress is going to be very unhappy with this. Driscoll was respected.”
Current and former defence officials have described Hegseth as consumed by paranoia, personal insecurity and even jealousy, angered when the spotlight falls on others such as Driscoll.

Driscoll, who was considered a potential successor to Hegseth should Trump fire the defence secretary, became the face of the Pentagon’s efforts to build up its arsenal of cheaper drones and efforts to develop more counter-drone and missile-defence technology.

Hegseth was “attempting to stymie transformation efforts” for personal reasons, said the person familiar with Driscoll’s thinking. The army under Driscoll tasked an infantry battalion to work on integrating drones but Hegseth ultimately ordered it dismantled.

While the army has taken the brunt of Hegseth’s changes, the navy is also under strain and facing budget pressure. Naval warfare has been at the centre of Trump and Hegseth’s military operations from the Caribbean to Iran, straining warships and depleting missiles.
Navy secretary John Phelan was fired in April. Trump on Tuesday nominated Hung Cao, the acting navy secretary and a former navy captain, to succeed him.

“It’s Secretary Hegseth who should be resigning after mishandling military operations in the Middle East and around the world,” Jeanne Shaheen, the Democratic senator from New Hampshire and a member of the armed services committee, told the FT.
“It is unimaginable that Secretary Hegseth is purging the ranks of top military officials at the same time that the US is in an ongoing conflict and as security challenges mount,” Shaheen added.
But despite the pressure mounting on the defence secretary from within the Pentagon and Republicans on Capitol Hill, Trump has continued to defend Hegseth.
Recommended

The president praised Hegseth when asked about speculation that the defence secretary might launch a 2028 White House run after a visit to Iowa. “He’s done a great job,” Trump said. “And right now, all he loves and all he cares about is the military and taking care of the military.”

Elissa Slotkin, a Democratic senator from Michigan and a member of the armed services committee, told CNN that Hegseth “has an audience of one that’s Donald Trump, and if someone disagrees with him or undercuts him or makes him look somehow weak, then he gets rid of them”.
“It does really start to feel like we’re on this never-ending purge,” Slotkin added.

macro_summary.paragraph_summary: The resignation of US Army Secretary Dan Driscoll, who cited personal animosity and interference from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, has deepened chaos at the Pentagon amid ongoing conflict with Iran and a sweeping purge of military leadership. Driscoll’s departure follows months of friction over military modernization, personnel decisions, and Hegseth’s removal of two dozen senior officers, including Army Chief of Staff General Randy George, sparking bipartisan concern over leadership instability and strategic mismanagement.
bullet_summary: US Army Secretary Dan Driscoll resigned after months of conflict with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, citing personal animosity and obstruction of military modernization.
Hegseth has purged over two dozen generals and admirals since Trump’s second term, including Army Chief of Staff General Randy George, triggering leadership vacuum and bipartisan alarm.
Driscoll’s exit leaves the army without a permanent secretary or chief of staff—critical roles requiring Senate confirmation—amid active combat operations in the Middle East.
Senate Republicans and former Pentagon officials warn that Hegseth’s leadership style, marked by purges and resistance to transformation, undermines military readiness and congressional trust.
Despite growing criticism from both parties and military leaders, President Trump continues to defend Hegseth, calling him a dedicated servant of the military.

opinion content. 
Growth is a life-and-death matter for Europe
articleContent: Last week, in the UN Detention Unit in The Hague, Ratko Mladić died. The Bosnian Serb former general was 84. Two contradictory thoughts occur.

First, Europe embarrassed itself in the 1990s. Sensing that its “hour” had come — a Luxembourg foreign minister’s phrase — the continent was going to manage the break-up of Yugoslavia without America. Subsequent chaos, including the war crimes for which Mladić was convicted, falsified that boast.

Second, those were the good old days of European military seriousness. In 1990, Britain spent 4 per cent of national output on defence. France spent 2.8 and Germany 2.5. On the eve of the Ukraine war, those numbers had fallen to 2.1 per cent, 1.9 and 1.3. The number of armed personnel collapsed in all three countries over the period.

So, just to restore a bad position, in which Europe was powerless to stop local atrocities, its leading countries have to raise defence spending. How? Except for Germany, none of them can borrow much more. (Britain’s public sector net debt was around 30 per cent in the 1990s. It is three times that now.) None can tax much more, at least not without damping incentives in their already subdued economies. Take the cash out of welfare, and voters revolt. The one answer is GDP growth. In fact, every European politician of good conscience should have a flowchart as their smartphone wallpaper. Growth —> tax receipts —> defence expenditure.

Until now, the case for growth was that, without it, Europe would become a bit poorer over time. This was never enough for voters to accept the upfront pain of, say, welfare cuts and lighter job protections. The prospect of national economic decline was too far off, and the starting point too high. So, reform packages came to almost nought: before Mario Draghi’s proposals stalled in 2024, the Lisbon Agenda stalled in 2000. Reforms that were enacted often proved electorally unsurvivable. Gerhard Schröder knows.

Now, the case for growth is that, without it, Europe cannot deter its mortal enemies. The economic question has become an existential one. The politics might be lining up for pro-growth reform, as it hasn’t for almost half a century.

As regular readers know, I am doubtful that rich and mature democracies can make painful reforms, except in a crisis. I just always assumed the crisis must be economic. The precedents suggest so: Britain’s humiliating IMF loan of 1976, the stagflation that gave rise to Reaganism, the market revolt against François Mitterrand’s government in France, the Eurozone crisis that spurred change in Greece and Spain. There is nothing like a bond sell-off to make even a deluded government wake up. The system works.

But what if the crisis is geopolitical? What if the impetus for change is to survive as a nation, not just to recover lost affluence? In that case, the proper historical parallel is the Meiji Restoration, when Japan modernised at light speed to save itself from conquest or vassalage. Unthinkable reforms, such as industrialisation, took on the air of patriotic necessity.

That was an imperial regime. The question is whether Europeans with a free vote will make the same connection between growth and survival. Perhaps, to nudge them along, governments will have The Conversation. That is, the seriousness of the Russian threat, and the holes in the existing defences against it, will be spelt out as never before. (In much of the east and north of the continent, voters need no such instruction.)

The risk here is huge. For one thing, being candid about unpreparedness is itself a security liability. Also, far-right parties will make hay, accusing the elite of exaggerating a remote problem to foist change on people. The Alternative for Germany is perhaps the western populist movement most inclined to see things from the Kremlin’s angle. It could win the region of Saxony-Anhalt this weekend. In this atmosphere, it is a rash liberal who confronts voters with the “grow or perish” case.

Alternatively, politicians need say very little. Events will do all the work. According to the German government, Russia was behind a drone attack at Leipzig airport last month. At some point, a “grey zone” event, perhaps in Britain, will be all too black. If the threat is serious, then almost by definition the public will notice. An equivalent of Commodore Matthew Perry stalking Tokyo Bay will happen. At that point, the need for growth will not be lost on even the most obtuse. Vladimir Putin will have done what Draghi couldn’t.

Either way, how Europe arrives at its Meiji moment matters less than getting there, and soon. It must become axiomatic that all priorities are subordinate to growth, because all priorities are subordinate to security.

Looking back, the peace dividend that Europe started to take in the 1990s has a worse reputation than it deserves. Spending a reduced share of GDP on defence is not total folly if that GDP is growing at a fast rate. The importance of the denominator gets lost in the obsession with Nato targets. What has left Europe so mortally exposed is its economic performance, especially since the crash, and especially in the countries big enough to make a military difference. The way out is, or should be, obvious. Europeans who have long pushed for growth might find that a clinching argument is at last on hand, even if time isn’t.
janan.ganesh@ft.com

macro_summary.paragraph_summary: Europe faces an existential crisis where economic growth is no longer just a path to prosperity but a prerequisite for national survival, driven by the urgent need to rebuild military strength in response to Russia's threat. The continent's defence spending has collapsed since the 1990s, and without significant GDP growth, it cannot afford the military modernisation required to deter aggression. This shift transforms growth from a long-term economic goal into a patriotic imperative, akin to Japan’s Meiji Restoration, demanding reforms that were previously politically unfeasible.
bullet_summary: Europe’s defence spending has plummeted since the 1990s, leaving it unable to deter threats from Russia.
Growth is now a national security imperative, not just an economic one, making it a matter of survival.
Historical parallels like the Meiji Restoration suggest that existential threats can drive rapid, transformative reform.
Political leaders face a high-risk challenge: either openly link growth to survival and risk backlash, or wait for a crisis to force change.
The failure to grow economically since the 2008 crash has left Europe dangerously unprepared, despite past promises of defence spending

paragraph_summaries.summary: Ratko Mladić’s death in The Hague detention unit evokes two conflicting reflections: Europe’s failed attempt to manage Yugoslavia’s breakup without U.S. help, and the irony that the 1990s were actually a time of greater European military seriousness.
Europe’s 1990s ambition to act independently in the Balkans was undermined by its inability to prevent war crimes, exposing the gap between its self-image and actual capacity.
In the 1990s, major European powers spent significantly more on defence than they do today, and their armed forces were much larger, but those levels have since declined sharply.
Restoring defence capability is now essential, but fiscal constraints limit borrowing and taxation; the only viable path is economic growth, which would boost tax revenues and fund military spending.
Previous calls for growth were dismissed by voters because economic decline felt distant and reforms were politically unsustainable, as seen in the failed Lisbon Agenda and Draghi’s stalled reforms.
The case for growth has shifted from economic improvement to national survival, potentially creating a rare political opening for pro-growth reforms.
Historically, democracies only enact painful reforms during crises, such as the 1976 UK IMF bailout or the Eurozone crisis, which forced change through economic pressure.
A geopolitical crisis, like the threat of invasion, could trigger reforms as rapidly as Japan’s Meiji Restoration, where national survival made modernisation a patriotic duty.
Governments may need to openly frame the Russian threat as a national emergency to justify growth-driven reforms, though this risks backlash from populist movements.
Populist parties, like Germany’s Alternative for Germany, may exploit fears of an exaggerated threat to discredit reform, making it politically dangerous to speak openly.
Alternatively, a major incident—such as a drone attack on a European airport—could force public awareness and acceptance of the need for growth, making crisis the true catalyst.
The timing and method of Europe’s transformation matter less than the urgency of achieving it, as growth must become the overriding priority for national security.
The post-Cold War peace dividend was not inherently flawed; it was sustainable only if growth remained strong, which it has not, leaving Europe dangerously exposed.
The long-standing push for growth now has a powerful new justification: without it, Europe cannot defend itself, and time is running out.
